[h1] Sound & Graphics: [/h1]
The game takes place all from a PC screen, the graphics are simple but are pleasing on the eye. The design of the UI is sleek and simple to understand. Orwell is accompanied by a soundtrack which now always gets stuck in my head. 

[h1] Gameplay: [/h1]
Once you realise how much is at stake and how much rests on the information that you mark you start to second guess each decison hoping you're going to get the desired outcome.

[h1] Replayablilty: [/h1]
There's a few different endings to the story. If you want to collect all the achievments you're going to have to repeat this 3 - 4 times, at least you'll get a new story though.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]
Good plotline
UI is very sleek and simple
Interesting characters 

[h1] Cons: [/h1]
Short gameplay
Not much replayability other than achivement hunting as the alternative endings aren't super interesting

[h1] Overall: [/h1]
A good time killer, I'd certainly reccomend picking Owell up although it may be best to wait until it goes on sale.

I recommend this game to anyone and everyone who's interested in law, civil rights, law enforcement, politics, technology, intelligence and counterintelligence. Although some can get through all five chapters quickly, this game gives a good feel for what investigators go through, and the impact their investigations can have on lives in the real world.  It also gives a good cyberexample of the "law of unintended consequences" that operates more often than not on legislation that starts out for the popular good in theory, but can be catastrophic in consequence when put into actual practice by the wrong minds or hands.

I predict that this will become a classic game series for all those who have interest in the subject matters I listed above.

So, where to get started ... Orwell was one of  the many games in my steam library collecting dust because I got it at some point but never got around to actually playing it. I picked it first over other games as I just started reading a book called '1984' by George Orwell. For anyone who enjoyed the book it's worth checking out the game. Although the book has a much better story in my opinion and if you enjoyed the game you really should check it out.

It took me about 5 hours for my first run. For me it was quite  an immersive experience and the game does a really good job at making you feel at the center of the plot. The story is not linear and the choices you make do feel like they actually matter unlike the old fallout games.  It was an interesting experience, but at some points the gameplay did hinder you with an obtrusive dialogue of your 'advisor', but not to the point if it becoming annoying.

To summarize without spoiling, it's about the future and ethics of our civilization and how we'll deal with privacy. Just as the book did, but in a simply numbed down version. The game is therefor not perfect, it lacked some depth in certain parts of the story. But the fact that you can go and play the game again will make the second time playing a complete different experience as you can now advance with knowledge of your previous playthrough which makes up for it.

~~==~~ 🐺 *Verdict* 🐺 ~~==~~
Should you get and play this game? Maybe, it's not for everyone. If you're interested in a more reading based game where choices matter that explores the future of privacy, than yes. In case you're not hyped about something like that I would still give the game a go if you can get it on sale

I found this game to be very interesting in concept, but a little lacking in execution.  The two main criticisms I have are related to the design of Orwell System itself I suppose.  Without spoiling anything, there are times where two 'conflicting' pieces of information need to be picked between in order to advance the story line down any given path.  However, in most cases this conflicting information isn't actually conflicting.  ie: A person did this one thing at time A, versus something completely else at time B.  Both of these statements could be inherently true, but must only one can be chosen as a fact.  I certainly understand why these choices are being presented to the player, and what they represent, but by accepting one as the truth, the Orwell System automatically eliminates the other as even a possibility.  A good investigator would accept both possible truths and investigate them for veracity and relevance, which is another flaw in the Orwell System; there is no verification and I suppose that's the point of the whole thing, but AS an IRL investigator, it bothers me to no end.  

The second issue I have with Orwell is that it can cherry pick information out of text which is likely relevant to a person I'm investigating, and it can tell me which person it's relevant to and even what the information represents, but the system isn't sophisticated enough to automatically assign that information to the relevant person??!  I have to manually choose that person from the suspect 'web' and then add the information.  If I don't the system tells me it's the wrong person.  If you know it's the wrong person, why not just put the information where it belongs??

Neither of these issues are game-breaking, and overall I enjoyed the 4 hours I spent figuring things out.  

A 'meta' issue I have with the Orwell System is how laughably unnecessary it is.  While the real-time information and telephone call intercepts were all incredibly helpful, a team of investigators using today's investigative techniques, with search warrants and without violating anybody's constitutional rights, likely could have come to the same conclusions.  A large amount of obtained information was all accessible on public webpages, and a check of a suspect's name, social media profiles, and close friend's social media would be the first stop in an investigation of this magnitude.

I did not expect this game to be as good as it was. None of the screenshots let me understand the limits and ramifications that the game system has in place, nor did I expect real-time sequences of information gathering and dissemination.

A+ will play again.

The Secretary Catherine Delacroix had to step down due to the revelation made by me about her positive acceptance of bombings which could play a good card to validate existence of surveillance over the population through the Orwell. Firstly I want to cover the mechanics of the game, which despite being few, are well implemented and easy to understand. You will basically make your own story from the data you get, as the other part will only get the info you send them you can send different things according to what you think is best... or worse. Despite being few important decisions, they DO impact the game, which does not happen in some other titles, and thats good. The game is based on that and will give you different approaches to how to obtain data, i.e. you can search the news, you can spy on peoples devices, or you can impersonate people on their online accounts. 
The main story is there, and you have to follow it to progress, but theres a true feeling of acomplishment with the decisions you make, since they seem to impact the story strongly, mainly for the outcome of the characters.

That being said, the whole point of the story is to show a really interesting point about reality, that everyone should hear about either on a game, a novel, a blog post, or whatever.

Next is the gameplay

Overall, this game is really interesting and I would recommend it for someone looking for a casual game to play.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a game where you play as an investigator hired outside the Nation. Your task is to discover a crime detail by searching from suspects' background information which you can gather around the web, to be later uploaded into Orwell security program. You will be accompanied by a single adviser in your every work session, their task will revolve around information that you put into Orwell, for them to act based on your input.

The game sets you into the day at the time a bombing is occurred at a public place. Your first day would revolve around investigating who's behind this bombing. You could work all-day long if you want and maybe put all the datachunks - highlighted information - available into Orwell [spoiler]since you are not "timed" until Episode 5[/spoiler], easy as is. But of course, the common ground is to double-check whether a datachunk is valid to your investigation, or they were there only as mere decorations of information scattered freely on web. Your understanding of validity will be tested, well, more or less.

The music managed to keep me into focus, with not too over-exaggerated tunes (listened to them on Spotify and looped them for some time). There are some tense moments - indicated by shock-therapy tune - where you have to choose which info is MORE valid among the other. You will be the judge of things revolving around the web information, but you know what to do. You have been trusted by the Nation to work with them, but are they trusted enough? Theoretically, they should be, giving the ability to build this seemingly-flawless program where you could uncover the truth of these people you're given task to keep an eye on.

Finishing the game, I'm telling you, they indeed work like a charm. Too well.

Oh, also low poly art-style. New term and style to adore in general.

Nitpicks that I have after discussing this with a fellow online investigator:
- I don't have any complaint for the mechanics, but I was hoping we could select our own datachunks instead of being presented in-game. [i]Then again it would be possibly overkill.[/i]
- Having voice actors for the call sessions would be nice, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]but then it was covered in the sequel which I have yet to get into.[/i][/url] So giving that one a pass.
- Calls and ongoing chats cannot be skipped during episode replay. I don't see a button or tutorial to archive the calls for later... [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]in which they covered this in the sequel, too.[/i][/url] This kills the will to replay the game under the same save file due to inefficiency, [i]unless it's not meant to punish the replayability?[/i]
- I read this somewhere, but calls and chats would start to roll AFTER we clicked on their names. Even when you left the game for coffee or lunch, it won't play until you click on it - making them "the most tolerate group of terrorists one has to deal with". [spoiler]The only uncontrollable moment is on the last episode's final call.[/spoiler]
Keep in mind I didn't need these to be implemented in the game - as they're all already covered in the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/]sequel[/url]. It would be too much of a work for the developers, as the game is already a success in the first place without these, anyway. 

Overall, Orwell managed to capture the feel of spying people to get info under the surface of the known. Which makes this game as one of my favorites, enough to delve deeper into privacy breach.

Orwell is engrossing and more than a bit disturbing considering the implications of some very real things that are happening in the world right now. More of an interactive novel than a proper game, it nonetheless pulled me in for the 3-4 hours it took to reach the end of it, as well as a couple of replays to try out different paths.

It's not perfect, though; there's no challenge in actually getting the information you require since it's highlighted for you and you simply have to upload it, which sort of takes most of the initiative out of your hands. You do get to decide how certain characters are viewed based on how much you pass on to the powers that be, and your choices affect how they're treated and what happens to them, but the prevailing narrative is more or less canned, on-rails, and you can't do very much to affect how it plays out other than within a narrow scope. Some of the decisions you make do have very profound consequences for the individuals concerned, and the first time through I did have a few things I deeply regretted because of what happened as a result.


The biggest downside is that the game is short and fairly linear; there are only so many branches/possibilties to explore, so once you've exhausted them, there's really not much replay value. 

I've seen a few comparisons made to Papers, Please, which is less slick to play but rather more profound to actually experience because of the huge number of variations in how it can go. Orwell comparatively lacks depth, but because you spend more time with all the characters and get to know them better (since you're snooping through their gadgets and availing yourself of some very personal details of their lives), what happens to them matters a lot more to you. At least, it mattered more to me. In Papers Please I was more concerned with getting myself and my family out of dodge. 

Think of Orwell as an interactive dystopian techno-thriller and you've got a pretty good idea what you're in for.

But there is basically no investigative work, hacking or anything that would be fun to do to find information. All the work is already done for you, every document is already analyzed, and you cannot investigate new people before being allowed to, even if it is clear they must have some role in the investigation.

So yes, the gameplay is overly simple and very linear, but maybe I could have been ok with it if I had found the story interesting.
But the story is boring. The main goal in the game (at least until I stopped playing) is to find the culprits responsible for a bomb attack. Sounds exciting right? Maybe the game becomes more complex and interesting later on (I really hope so), but I am just not interested enough so far in the story to continue playing. Maybe I'll try again later...

Orwell is a very unique game.  The player takes the persona of an investigator in a futuristic 1984-style society and tries to find information/evidence regarding some terrorist bombings.  There are 5 chapters in the game which take you on a journey.  The first chapter you are closely led by your examiner, but then more and more choices are laid before you as you delve into websites, eavesdrop on phone calls and investigate hard drives.  

The game is somewhat linear and the main choice is to choose if information is relevant or not to the case and avoiding taking things out of context.  For once you claim something is true, it is stuck in stone.  

Overall, playing Orwell (after the first 60 minutes) became a highly engrossing experience.  The delivery is very well done and even builds to a massive tension where getting information at one point is almost frantic as you are listening to a phone call.  I won't give the details away, but it was tense and somewhat chilling conclusion.  

Overall, a very unique game, full of reading text, but well-delivered. 

7/10 Recommended.

There's several overarching themes in Orwell - technology, totalitarianism, propaganda, identity - and Orwell blends them quite well. It's akin to a visual novel, with the story unfolding as you choose what to upload to the Orwell  program and seeing how your choices affect the story. Though that is also its weakness.

Orwell's systems are displayed as "datachunks", uploadable bits of information to fill out a person's profile. However, those datachunks are pre-highlighted, bringing the only gameplay decision to be "Do I upload info 1 or info 2?". Finding new information feels less like being a detective and more like rote drag-and-drop to progress the story. Important datachunks are highlighted, the media it's in is also highlighted and you have your handler telling you which media to check. There's no skill involved.

Overall the story is interesting and well-presented, but gameplay lets it down. Other games present similar themes and gameplay better. If you want more totalitarianism, Papers Please is a better example of it. If you want to feel like a detective, Her Story or Return of the Obra Dinn do those aspects far better. If you want a quick, good story then buy Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You.

The game sounded really interesting but after 2 hours of playtime I refunded it. The idea that you hunt for information and decide what to pass on and what to keep private is a nice way of turning a game into a subtle reference to personal bias. A clever idea that could have been great. The problem is that, certainly for the 2 hours I played, that simply wasn't the case. There is no hunting for information. It is handed to you on a plate. The basic routine is this:

A page of information is loaded and appears on the right of the screen. Important parts of the text are highlighted. Click the highlighted text and drag it to the Orwell upload facility on the left of the screen. Drag enough pieces of text and a new page of information is presented to you with highlighted parts. Drag and drop. New page. Drag and drop. New page.

You will discover social media handles. Great, now you can hunt the person down and..oh wait, no their feed just gets presented to you with highlighted text. Drag and drop.

You manage to get the telephone number of a suspect. Now you can tap their line and listen in on their conversations. Oh wait, it just gets presented to you, no action required. Never mind, look, there's the symbol to say they are about to have a conversation. QUICK, check in and listen to them before they...oh wait, no. You can simply ignore the symbol for half an hour and then check it, because the messages only start when you open up the screen. If these really are terrorists, they are the most considerate ones on the planet as they refuse to start their conversation until you are listening in. Try to keep up? No need, go make a drink, come back and find the page of text. Ignore the drivel, the important bits are highlighted.  Drag and drop.

Still, your decisions about what to upload is really what the game is about. Except that even in those first 2 hours there were a few occasions where I decided not to upload something because it appeared to be out of context. A message displaying agressiveness or hatred of the state, but in the context of the document it seemed to be just social media waffle and not really genuine terrorist. So I didn't upload it. Result? Nothing. The game simply wouldn't progress until I uploaded it. The choice was removed. So after a while of hunting and finding no new clues I reluctantly uploaded the info and lo and behold a new page of information was presented to me. Drag and drop. Rinse and repeat.

Clearly a lot of people have found something great in this game and I truly love the concept but I cannot recommend it for what it claims to be.  If you are looking for the perfect Drag and Drop Simulator to spend your evenings on though, you can't go wrong here.
